question.text: A hydrogen-like atom (atomic number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi></math>) is in a higher excited state of quantum number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></math>. This excited atom can make a transition to the first excited state by successively emitting two photons of energies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>10.20</mtext><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>17.00</mtext><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math> respectively. Alternatively, the atom from the same excited state can make a transition to the second excited state by successively emitting two photons of energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>4.25</mtext><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>5.95</mtext><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math> respectively. Determine the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi></math>. [Ionization energy of hydrogen atom <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>=</mo><mtext>13.6</mtext><mo> </mo><mi>eV]</mi></math>

solution.text:
10.2+17=13.6×Z2122-1n2;      4.25+5.95=13.6×Z2132-1n2

Solving the above two equation we get, Z=3 and n=6.
